content: Fuchsine, also known as rosaniline hydrochloride, is a magenta dye with the chemical formula C20H19N3·HCl. When dissolved in water, it exhibits a magenta color, while in its solid form, it appears as dark green crystals. This compound is not only used for dyeing textiles but also serves as a staining agent for bacteria and, occasionally, as a disinfectant. There are other chemically similar formulations sold under the name fuchsine, and the molecule is known by several dozen synonyms. The name fuchsine was given by its original manufacturer, Renard frères et Franc, and is typically attributed to one of two etymologies. It may derive from the color of the flowers of the plant genus Fuchsia, named in honor of the botanist Leonhart Fuchs. Alternatively, it could be a German translation of the French name Renard, which means fox and translates to Fuchs in German. An 1861 article in Répertoire de Pharmacie stated that the name was chosen for both reasons. Acid fuchsine is a mixture of homologues of basic fuchsin, modified by the addition of sulfonic groups. This modification results in twelve possible isomers, all of which are considered satisfactory despite slight differences in their properties. Basic fuchsine is a mixture of rosaniline, pararosaniline, and Magenta II. Formulations intended for the preparation of Schiff reagent must have a high content of pararosaniline. The exact composition of basic fuchsine can vary depending on the vendor and batch, which makes different batches more or less suitable for specific applications. When combined with phenol as an accentuator, it is referred to as carbol fuchsin and is used for staining the bacterium responsible for tuberculosis.
